title: What is `self` in a Python method?
front: What is `self` in a Python method?
back: The specific object the method was called on. obj.method(x) is translated to Class.method(obj, x), so the instance is passed in automatically as the first argument. It is not a global or class namespace.

title: List vs tuple: the differences that matter
front: List vs tuple: the differences that matter
back: A list is mutable (append, change items); a tuple is immutable. A tuple of hashable items is hashable, so it can be a dict key or a set member; a list cannot. Use a tuple for a fixed record such as (row, col).

title: What goes wrong with a mutable default argument, e.g. def add(x, items
front: What goes wrong with a mutable default argument, e.g. def add(x, items=[])?
back: The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and shared by every call. Items pile up across calls. Fix: items=None, then `if items is None: items = []` inside.

title: Instance attribute vs class attribute
front: Instance attribute vs class attribute
back: An instance attribute is set on self (usually in __init__) and belongs to one object. A class attribute is defined in the class body and shared by all instances. A mutable class attribute, like a list, is shared state: a classic bug.

title: @classmethod vs @staticmethod vs a normal method: when to use each?
front: @classmethod vs @staticmethod vs a normal method: when to use each?
back: Normal method: needs the instance (self). @classmethod: receives the class (cls); use for alternative constructors such as from_csv. @staticmethod: receives neither; a helper function that lives in the class for organisation only.

title: What does super().__init__(...) do, and what happens if a subclass for
front: What does super().__init__(...) do, and what happens if a subclass forgets it?
back: It runs the parent class's __init__ so the parent's attributes get set. If the subclass defines __init__ and does not call it, the parent's attributes are missing and the first method that uses them raises AttributeError.

title: What is an abstract base class, and what do ABC and @abstractmethod en
front: What is an abstract base class, and what do ABC and @abstractmethod enforce?
back: A class that defines an interface and cannot be instantiated. With `class Model(ABC)` and `@abstractmethod def fit(...)`, calling Model() raises TypeError, and so does instantiating any subclass that has not implemented every abstract method.

title: __repr__ vs __str__, and why define __eq__ and __hash__ together?
front: __repr__ vs __str__, and why define __eq__ and __hash__ together?
back: __repr__ is the unambiguous developer view (shown in the REPL and inside containers); __str__ is the readable view for print, and falls back to __repr__. Defining __eq__ alone sets __hash__ to None, so objects can no longer go in sets or dict keys. Equal objects must have equal hashes.

title: Bayes' theorem, and the two-box check
front: Bayes' theorem, and the two-box check
back: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B), where P(B) = sum over all cases of P(B|case) P(case). Box 1 has 3 blue of 10, box 2 has 6 blue of 10, boxes equally likely: P(box 1 | blue) = (0.3 x 0.5) / (0.3 x 0.5 + 0.6 x 0.5) = 1/3.

title: Derive the MLE for a coin: 450 heads in 1000 tosses
front: Derive the MLE for a coin: 450 heads in 1000 tosses
back: Likelihood L(p) = p^k (1-p)^(n-k). Log: k log p + (n-k) log(1-p). Derivative: k/p - (n-k)/(1-p) = 0. Solve: p = k/n = 0.45. The steps are always likelihood, log, derivative, set to zero.

title: Cross-entropy (log loss) for binary classification: formula and why
front: Cross-entropy (log loss) for binary classification: formula and why
back: Loss = -[y log(p) + (1-y) log(1-p)], averaged over rows. It is the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model, so minimising it is maximum likelihood. The log punishes confident wrong predictions very hard: p = 0.01 for a true 1 costs 4.6, p = 0.5 costs 0.69.

title: How do you fit linear regression: closed form and the alternative?
front: How do you fit linear regression: closed form and the alternative?
back: Closed form (normal equations): beta = (X'X)^-1 X'y, from setting the gradient of squared error to zero. Alternative: gradient descent, beta = beta - lr x gradient, where the gradient of mean squared error is (2/n) X'(X beta - y). Use it when the data are too big to invert X'X.

title: A geo experiment is contaminated: a second channel raised spend in the
front: A geo experiment is contaminated: a second channel raised spend in the treated regions. Effect on the estimate, and the fix?
back: The measured effect is biased towards zero, because the other channel replaced part of the lost conversions. The extra uncontrolled spend adds noise, so the standard error is if anything larger, and it does not show the bias. Fix: regress on the region-by-week panel with the other channel's spend as a covariate, or difference-in-differences against the pre-period.

title: More features than rows: why does least squares fail, and what does ri
front: More features than rows: why does least squares fail, and what does ridge do?
back: With p > n, X'X cannot be inverted, so there are infinitely many perfect fits. Ridge adds lambda to the diagonal (penalty lambda x sum of beta squared), which makes it solvable and shrinks coefficients towards zero. Lasso (absolute-value penalty) sets some exactly to zero, selecting features.

title: How does a tree choose a split, in classification and in regression?
front: How does a tree choose a split, in classification and in regression?
back: Classification: the split that most reduces impurity, measured by Gini (1 - sum of p squared) or entropy. Regression: the split that most reduces variance (squared error) of the target. Gini is not used for regression.

title: KNN vs K-means in one line each
front: KNN vs K-means in one line each
back: KNN is supervised: predict from the k nearest labelled points, no training step. K-means is unsupervised: cluster unlabelled points around k centroids by alternating assign and re-centre.

title: Vanishing and exploding gradients: what and the standard fixes
front: Vanishing and exploding gradients: what and the standard fixes
back: In deep networks, backpropagation multiplies many derivatives. Below 1 they shrink to nothing (early layers stop learning); above 1 they blow up. Fixes: ReLU-type activations, residual connections, normalisation layers, careful initialisation, and gradient clipping for explosion.

title: What does attention compute, in one sentence, and the three parts?
front: What does attention compute, in one sentence, and the three parts?
back: For each token, a weighted average of all tokens' values, where the weights come from how well this token's query matches every token's key (dot product, scaled, then softmax). Query: what I am looking for. Key: what I offer. Value: what I pass on.

title: Type I vs Type II error in null-hypothesis language
front: Type I vs Type II error in null-hypothesis language
back: Type I: rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive); its rate is alpha, usually 5%. Type II: failing to reject a false null (a miss); its rate is beta, and power = 1 - beta, usually 80%.

title: Time complexity of: dict lookup, `x in list`, sorting, and a nested lo
front: Time complexity of: dict lookup, `x in list`, sorting, and a nested loop over an n-by-m grid
back: Dict or set lookup: O(1) on average. `x in list`: O(n). Sorting: O(n log n). Nested loop over a grid: O(n x m). Summing each h-by-w window from scratch: O(n m h w); a 2D prefix-sum table makes each window O(1).

title: A/B test on a rare final action (e.g. cancellations): where in the fun
front: A/B test on a rare final action (e.g. cancellations): where in the funnel do you enrol users, and why?
back: As close to the action as possible. Enrol at landing and only about 1% of users ever reach the step, so 99% of the sample adds noise and no signal; the effect is diluted and the test runs far longer. Enrol at the cancel click and the baseline rate is 10 to 15%, so the same effect is detectable with a fraction of the users. Rule: randomise where the experience first differs.

title: Define A, B (and C) for a proposed change in one sentence each. What m
front: Define A, B (and C) for a proposed change in one sentence each. What must every variant definition contain?
back: A (control) = today's experience, unchanged. B (treatment) = the same experience with exactly ONE thing changed. C = a second version of that one thing (not a second idea). Each definition needs: who is eligible, the unit that is randomised, the single difference, and the metric it should move. If you cannot say the single difference in one sentence, the test is not designed yet.

title: Marketing attribution: a booking follows three touchpoints. Name the a
front: Marketing attribution: a booking follows three touchpoints. Name the approaches for splitting the credit, from simplest to data-driven.
back: Rule-based: last-click (all credit to the last touch), first-click, linear (equal split), position-based (most to first and last), time-decay (more to recent touches). Data-driven: Markov chain removal effect (how much conversion drops if a channel is removed from the paths) and Shapley value (a channel's average marginal contribution over all orderings). Attribution describes credit; only an experiment (geo or holdout) measures incrementality.

title: Feature importance inside a gradient-boosted model: what are split cou
front: Feature importance inside a gradient-boosted model: what are split count and gain, and what is the catch?
back: Split count (weight) = how many times a feature is used to split. Gain = the total reduction in the training loss from those splits. Both come from the training data, so they favour high-cardinality and continuous features and split the credit between correlated ones. They also depend on the loss being optimised: change the objective and the ranking changes. For a ranking you will act on, use permutation importance on held-out data or SHAP.

title: Gradient descent: the update rule, and batch vs stochastic vs mini-bat
front: Gradient descent: the update rule, and batch vs stochastic vs mini-batch.
back: Update: parameter = parameter minus learning rate times the gradient of the loss. Too large a learning rate overshoots or diverges; too small crawls. Batch: gradient over all rows per step (exact, slow). Stochastic (SGD): one row per step (noisy, cheap, can escape shallow dips). Mini-batch: a small batch (e.g. 32 to 512) per step, the default in practice: smooth enough and fits on a GPU. One pass over all the data is an epoch.

title: Regularisation in deep learning: dropout, batch normalisation, and the
front: Regularisation in deep learning: dropout, batch normalisation, and the other standard tools.
back: Dropout: during training, switch off a random share of units each step so the network cannot lean on any single one; at prediction time all units are on. Batch normalisation: rescale each layer's inputs to a stable mean and spread per mini-batch; it speeds up and stabilises training and regularises a little. Also: weight decay (L2 on the weights), early stopping on a validation set, data augmentation.

title: A convolutional network (CNN): the three kinds of layer and what each
front: A convolutional network (CNN): the three kinds of layer and what each does.
back: Convolution: slide small filters over the input; each filter detects a local pattern (an edge, a texture) wherever it appears, with shared weights. Pooling: shrink the feature map (e.g. keep the max of each 2 by 2 block), giving some tolerance to small shifts. Fully connected: at the end, combine the detected features into the prediction. Early layers find simple patterns, deeper layers combinations of them.

title: RAG vs fine-tuning: what does each change, when do you use which, and
front: RAG vs fine-tuning: what does each change, when do you use which, and what is LoRA?
back: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) changes WHAT the model knows at answer time: retrieve relevant documents and put them in the prompt. Use it for facts that change or are private, and when answers must cite sources. Fine-tuning changes HOW the model behaves: tone, format, a narrow skill. It does not keep facts fresh. LoRA is cheap fine-tuning: freeze the original weights and train small low-rank matrices added to them. Order in practice: prompt first, then RAG, then fine-tune.

title: How do you evaluate an LLM application in production?
front: How do you evaluate an LLM application in production?
back: Quality: groundedness (is the answer supported by the retrieved context), hallucination rate, task success on a fixed test set, with an LLM as judge calibrated against human labels. Retrieval, for RAG: does the right document come back (recall at k). Operations: latency, cost per request (tokens, and the number of calls for agents), failure rate. Risk: human review for high-stakes outputs, and monitoring of real traffic for drift.
